newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION-S.African Aug exchequer crunch-By E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-S.African Aug exchequer crunch-By E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

JOHANNESBURG, Aug 15 - As at the end of June 1997 the total nominal value of the local registered stock (LRS) liabilities of government stood at 285.7 billion rand, which in a full year would pay out 33.3 billion rand in interest on a cash flow basis, that is excluding any accrued interest on the zero-coupon stocks which amounted to a redemption value of 13.8 billion rand.

With interest being paid half-yearly the peak months of interest payments are August and February, when 8.4 billion rand is due to be paid out. September and March payments are next highest at 3.2 billion rand each, followed by November and May at 1.7 billion, etc.

More precisely, the February 1998 cash payment will be 613 million rand less on account of the redemption of the R119 stock this August, but this will be offset by the interest on whatever replacement stocks are issued in respect of the R119.

The major cash interest payments in August will be on the 28th of 3.2 billion rand for the R150 and on the 31st of 4.2 billion rand for the R153, that is 7.4 billion rand in the course of 4 days at the very end of the month.

In addition to the cash interest payments on the LRS stocks there will, of course, be interest payments on other forms of debt and the discounts to be credited in the books in respect of Treasury bills issued in the month. But the major additional disbursement in the month is the redemption of the R119 on the 15th, amounting to 8,761 million rand, in addition to the redemption of the Z100 amounting to 145 million rand on the 21st.

In all, 17.3 billion rand has to be disbursed by the Exchequer for the cash interest and redemption transactions in respect of LRS in August. It may be noted that a redemption of zero-interest stock, amounting to 2,663 million rand, is due in September in addition to the 3.2 billion rand of cash interest then which, in itself, is a fairly substantial outflow.

It is virtually impossible to predict normal revenue and expenditure figures for a particular month, but on the basis of the pattern of growth to date in this fiscal year, there could be at least a billion rand deficit of non-interest expenditure over revenues. So the Exchequer is facing a cash flow deficit of a minimum 18 billion rand, perhaps as much as 19 billion rand, in the month.

On the face of it this would appear to be a formidable problem. However, it is manageable on the assumption that, in effect, the R119 is going to be rolled over through appropriate sales of the two major funding stocks, the R153 and the R157 and, maybe, mopped up through Treasury bills. The interest payments and the remaining non-interest expenditure deficit will have to be financed in principle through the running down of cash balances.

At the end of July the balance in the Exchequer account with the Reserve Bank amounted to 1,317 million rand and the net balance in the Tax and Loan accounts with the commercial banks amounted to 7,777 million rand. In addition there were foreign balances amounting to 2,218 million rand from the proceeds of the Yankee loan in June. Assuming these will have been sold to the Reserve Bank during the course of August the effective amount on balance with the Reserve Bank will have been 3,535 million rand.

Possible action then by the end of August is a full run down of the Tax and Loan account balances and a reduction in Exchequer account balances by up to 1.6 billion rand. But there are still problems in that sufficient cash balances have to be held at the end of the month for transfers to the provinces early in September - of the order of at least 3.5 billion rand. Alternatives will have to be sought through an even greater volume of Treasury bills, or running into overdraft with the banks. It has to be noted that there was a Reserve Bank loan to government of 625 million rand for the first time in July and this could be the thin end of the wedge as far as monetisation of the budget is concerned.

Insofar as there are drawings from the Exchequer account there should be a corresponding reduction of the money market shortage and an easing of money market rates. This is likely to happen at the very end of the month.

Also of considerable interest will be the impact on the money supply. In principle the transfer of balances from government's accounts to those of the private sector will impact on the money supply. This should rise sharply and reverse the situation that emerged in June when, despite a 7.8 billion rand rise in bank credit, money supply fell by 0.5 billion rand. The actual impact on the money supply will only be known towards the end of September, which is another reason for not expecting any move on Bank rate before then.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
